utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, with Judge Morrison away due to his urgent matters. You haven't finished, Mr. Karadzic? Do we have Mr. Durmic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We haven't started with him yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Durmic. Would you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Durmic, before you start giving evidence, I'd like to draw your attention to a particular Rule here at the Tribunal. Under this Rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the accused, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you may say may amount to an admission of your guilt for having offended an offence, a criminal offence, or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you believe that your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Durmic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, your Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Durmic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you and to remind myself to make a pause between what I say and what you say so that everything is recorded on the transcript, and to speak slowly so we don't have to make corrections to the record, because that is a waste of time. Mr. Durmic, did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see in e-court 1D7218, please. 7218.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see that statement on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read this statement and signed it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we see the last page to identify the signature. Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement accurately reflect what you said in that interview to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: In essence, yes, but there are things I could add regarding the pre-war period in the area of Milici municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us this now.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I want to emphasise that the leadership of the municipality and the leadership of the Boksit enterprise invested great efforts in the negotiations with the Muslim population of Stedrici and Djile and other villages located on the route from Milici to the mine to avoid a war. All the employees of Muslim ethnicity were told that they are encouraged to return to their work in the Boksit company and to get involved in the restoration of the production of the ore, because we had international contracts already signed, and any delay in the production and any interruptions caused losses. A couple of dozen tonnes of flour and other supplies were delivered to that population. Delegations to sent to negotiate with them because they never wanted to come for negotiations to our premises. I worked in the security detail for these negotiations together with other policemen. And the population was willing to accept the offer to return to their work and to continue normal co-existence. However, there were a couple of extremist leaders who exerted great pressure on their own Muslim people and did not let them carry out all these agreements. People were blackmailed, and we have statements to confirm this. People were told that their families would be killed, and there was even one statement that I believe is mentioned in my own which says that they were told, "If you don't want to join our units, we'll bring six men from Sandzak who will kill all your family members." Furthermore, I want to stress that from these villages that I enumerated, by the end of May the population had come to the bank and collected their salaries without any impediment, and as one of the Muslims says in his statement, "We continued making this trip until we were warned by the men at the roadblock in Jokovaca that we cannot go there anymore. And a couple of days after this prohibition of passage at the roadblocks, these people, including one man who worked in the Boksit company, made the request for accommodation to be found for them, all these people who were getting called up in the mobilisation. All these people found refuge in the secondary school in Derventa, and in my estimate there were about a hundred of them. Food was brought to them. Clothes were brought to them. Mothers with children were put up there, and, of course, we put up physical security around the centre so that these people would not be threatened or put in any jeopardy. And that day, around 10.00 p.m., it was drizzling. The security men noticed a group of people approaching the facility, and one of them were -- was captured. He was found to have explosive devices in a bag he was carrying. Pieces of slow-burning fuse were found on these explosives, and this man said that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch all the names of the Muslim leaders.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- who have sent these men to attack the centre and then blame the Serbs. That night we had to evacuate the people from that facility because we were no longer able to guarantee their safety, and then again in agreement with their representatives, we talked about where they want to go and where they would feel the safest, because that location was no longer safe. Nobody wanted to be responsible if anything happened. So in the course of that night, with police escort we bused them to Zaklopaca settlement where some of them rejoined their families, whereas others were put up in the primary school. They remained there for another day or two, and then they continued in the direction of Tuzla or wherever they had family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the situation with medical services and trade? How long did all this continue to operate in Milici and how?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: I've said previously that at the beginning of May, they were still able to come to the bank and collect their salaries, which means that they could also go shopping. There were no problems. As for health services, I remember one case when the conflict was already going on, a young man, wounded, was brought by his own brother. I don't know what he said, that Serbs or territorial men injured him or maybe it was a self-inflicted injury, but he was taken by ambulance to the military hospital in Sokolac, and in that statement I read he died during transport. He was driven by an ambulance with proper medical staff around him, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Taking into account these additions, does this statement now accurately reflect what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Well, this statement mainly reflects the pre-war situation in our municipality, Milici, and the relations between the Serb and the Muslim population and the approach taken by the leadership of the municipality towards these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to ask you the same questions today as when you were giving the statement, would your answers be essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Essentially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this 92 package, 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, I'd like to deal with associated exhibits one by one in light of the ruling that I gave last year, in particular with respect to third-party statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We're only offering five associated exhibits at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we deal with it one by one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And we ask that all of them or whichever ones you admit be added to our 65 ter list as we didn't have the witness -- the witness had not been interviewed as of the time of our filing of our exhibit list. The first one that we're offering is 1D7018.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Then 1D7019.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: 1D7020, 1D7021, and finally, 1D7214.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no objection to all of the associated exhibits just mentioned by Mr. Robinson, although we would query the relevance of 1D07018, which is the report of an on-site investigation about an attack which we would say would be tu quoque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether it's tu quoque or not, but the paragraph can be understood without that exhibit, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So are you minded to withdraw that exhibit as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not really because we think it corroborates his information, but if you don't think of it's of valuable to the Chamber that's up to you, but we think it's corroborative of the information in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While it may be corroborative, it is the Chamber's view that the -- it does not form indispensable, inseparable part of the statement as such. So if we would not admit it -- admit it as part of associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I say something, Excellency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary, you may tell us the relevance and you may lead it live. We are not admitting it as part of associated exhibits. So we will be admitting those four associated exhibits, and what to do with the paragraphs that are related to the exhibit that were not tendered, I would like the parties to discuss to redact some part of the statement or not. I leave it to the parties. Ms. Sutherland, do you follow? If you could liaise with Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we give the numbers for those.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the 92 ter statement will -- 65 ter number 1D7218 will be Exhibit D2944. And 65 ter number 1D7019 will be Exhibit D2945. 7020 will be Exhibit 2946; 1D7021 will be Exhibit 2947; and 65 ter number 1D7214 will be Exhibit D2948.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, precisely on the example of this municipality, Vlasenica, the Prosecution has tried to represent my speech as the trigger for the further chain of events, my speech at that funeral, whereas the events described are much more convincing as the trigger. It is not about tu quoque. It is about finding out the reason why things happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The term "associated exhibit" is a kind of term of art. In order to be admitted as part of the associated exhibit, it should be forming an indispensable and inseparable part of the statement. Please consult with Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now I would read a summary of statement of Mr. Zoran Durmic in English, and then we'll see whether to lead this document live. Mr. Zoran Durmic was an inspector of the crime prevention police in the SJB Vlasenica. Before the war, he was assigned to the reserve police of Vlasenica Public Security Station. Before the war, as a reserve, Zoran Durmic would take part in training exercises and listen to lectures. Sometimes in mid-September 1991, he received a mobilisation call-up to report to the Vlasenica SJB. He was assigned on this occasion because the situation between the Serbs and Muslims was very complicated. Current members of active-duty policemen could not guarantee the security of the population so that authorities were forced to mobilise the reserve police force of which both Serbs and Muslims were members. Mr. Zoran Durmic and his colleagues worked every day in shifts patrolling the town of Milici, making the population seem more secure. He spent a month or two in this position, until the security situation improved. However, he was mobilised once again in March 1992. The situation this time was much more dramatic the as there were already armed clashes between Serbs and Muslims in some neighbouring municipalities. The JNA was also withdrawing from Croatia via Bosnia to Serbia, and columns of military vehicles passed through Milici every day. On 5th of April, 1992, Zoran Durmic received an order to escort a military convoy to Mali Zvornik in Serbia along with two other officers, Radomir Pantic and Mirko Lekovic. The officers travelled in an official police car. However, on the way, they came to a Muslim barricade manned by Muslim policemen and one Muslim soldier among them was an active policeman. The convoy was stopped at the barricade and questioned. The Muslim officers were rude, and it was clear that they disliked the JNA. Eventually, they let the convoy pass, and about a kilometre behind the barricade, the convoy came across a second barricade, this time manned by the Serb Territorial Defence. The Territorial Defence moved the barricade and allowed the convoy to pass unhindered. The officers experienced abusive behaviour by the Muslims on their return journey, and when the officers returned to Milici, they saw that a large crowd had gathered in front of the police station. They were told that the crowd had gathered as the police were distributing weapons to the Muslims. The next day, Zoran Durmic again was requested to accompany the same two officers to Banja Koviljaca and Zvornik to reclaim a car that had been taken from an officer by Muslim forces the day before. On the way, they encountered a car positioned across the highway blocking their way. As they approached, a number of armed Muslim soldiers jumped out of the bushes. They were all armed with automatic rifles, and the officers were ordered to get out of the car. The Muslims took the police officers' pistols and automatic rifles. The Muslims also took the police car that the officers had been travelling in. Zoran Durmic noted that the soldiers were well armed, dressed in new camouflage uniforms, and had modern walkie-talkies. The police officers requested to speak to their superiors, and after a while two further men arrived. The Muslim -- Muslim forces wanted one of the police officers to negotiate a cease-fire with Arkan. However, they were told it was not possible. At this moment, a man named Medo appeared, and he said that he would take the officers as far as Kasaba to allow them to get home. The police officers were mistreated at other barricades on their journey home, and after this incident, Zoran Durmic realised that the war with the Muslims was inevitable. On 21st of January, 1992, the Muslims ambushed a TAM truck transporting workers to the Boksit mine. Eight Serbian workers including two women were killed. Another incident followed soon after the 27th of May, 1992, when the Muslims carried out an ambush of some Boksit drivers. Five drivers were killed and the trucks burned. These incidents made the people in Milici uneasy. After these incidents, daily attacks against Serbian villages in Milici municipality were carried out. All the Serbian villages were burned to the ground and the population expelled, killed, or wounded, and their property looted. Zoran Durmic is not aware that the incident of 16th of May, 1992, was planned or organised. It was a place where the Muslims attacked strongly and the fighting went on for several hours. On 13th of July, 1995, whilst on duty, Zoran Durmic noted that a large group of Muslims were being guarded by the army. There were wounded men among them, and they were being treated by the medical personnel of the hospital in Milici. Whilst they were in the area, there were no killings of Muslim captives. They were being transported by buses away from Milici, and no one stopped these buses or removed persons from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Durmic, now I would like to ask you this: The Prosecution cited my speech of the 29th of September, 1992, at the funeral of Serbs massacred in Rogosija as if that agreement incited towards hatred and intolerance in Vlasenica. Whether any events before that speech of mine that had an effect on the atmosphere among the people, particularly the Serb people, and for inter-ethnic relations in Milici and Vlasenica. This is the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Well, first, perhaps we could go back to the reading of my statement. Perhaps there's an error in the interpretation. It says "public security station," but actually it's a station sector Milici. We were a branch, station branch, in Milici that was part of the police station in Vlasenica. So until the police station in Milici was formed, we carried out all the police work. And then it says that on the outskirts of Zvornik, in front of the police station we intercepted a large group of people --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch everything that the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Durmic, I think you spoke a bit too fast for the interpreters to catch up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Durmic, may I just ask you, what I read is not an exhibit. If it's correct in the statement, don't pay any attention to what I read in the summary. If the statement is accurate, then everything is all right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember my question?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: For the record, the Prosecution wasn't put on notice of this evidence which is about to be led in relation to Mr. Karadzic's speech.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It pertains to the associated exhibit that we decided to lead live, Milici. So we did not need to provide notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not entirely correct. We should be put on notice as to what evidence will be led from the witness whether live or pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When -- when the Defence is tendering certain exhibit or is planning to tender a certain exhibit, is it obliged to tell the other party the purpose of such tendering? Probably it's -- would you like to respond to what Mr. Karadzic just stated?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, he was asking the witness about his speech in September 1992. Now, whatever the witness says about that speech, we have not been put on notice anywhere in the Rule 65 ter summary or in the statement of what the witness will say about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understood his statement to be the reason why he's tendering 1D7018. Mr. Tieger? You can't resist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I -- that's exactly right, Mr. President. Not when it implicates an issue that was raised previously and then has a bearing on notice in the future. So I simply wanted to say that it -- we're talking about potentially two different things. The -- there may not be a rule that says that one party is obliged to explain to the other in advance the purpose of tendering a particular exhibit, but there is a rule that says that the other party has to be provided with notice of the facts upon which the witness will testify. Excuse me. Now, it may be the case that sometimes the notification that a particular exhibit will be tendered overlaps between the two, and so I'm not speak -- I'm not pre-empting anybody speaking to this particular issue but, it continues to be the case that in the face of deficient 65 ter summaries and belated submission of statements - I'm not suggesting that this is one - that then the Defence will advance information or elicit information from a witness without any notification to the Prosecution whatsoever, thereby disrupting and undermining the opportunity to prepare for cross. So I'm simply saying that as before, the issue is one of whether the Prosecution has been provided with sufficient notice under Rule 65 ter about the facts upon which the witness will testify so that it may properly prepare. I apologise for not be able to resist, but it is a significant issue, one that's been raised on many occasions, and I think that's a distinction which is useful to bear in mind here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if I may add, Your Honour, I didn't see the connection between 1D17018, which is about an incident in June and Mr. Karadzic's question which was about his speech in September, and he uses -- and he even referred to the end of 1992 in his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we hear from you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think the best thing to do is to put the document before the witness and we'll avoid all of this problem. This was Dr. Karadzic's way of introducing the document. I think that's the problem. The Prosecution -- for what Dr. Karadzic is intending to do, which is to admit the document that was offered as an associate exhibit, I don't think this raises any broader issues of notice if his question is understood in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could tell Mr. Karadzic to proceed in that way, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we call up 1D7018 in e-court, please. Had this document been accepted as an associated exhibit, I would have discussed it in my closing arguments. But now I would like to see what was going on in June, much earlier than September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what this document is, Mr. Durmic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: This is a document which is a record of an on-site investigation in the village of Rupovo Brdo, the municipality of Milici, which was burned down by Muslim forces on the 10th of June, 1992. This village was where five people were killed. Some even had their necks cut. And then after 21 years, three persons are registered as missing. Unfortunately they have still not been found. This is a father and son, Trivko and Zugic Komljanin [phoen] and Milinkovic Vlado. This village was completely blocked for a few days and it was not possible to conduct the on-site investigation right away. I also might note that all of these victims were buried without any religious rites, without any previous medical examination, so that we don't have any medical documents about the injuries or wounds on the bodies of those killed but on the basis of statements and their close relatives we noted these.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the next page, please. You say here in the first paragraph that the whole village was burnt to the ground, including the barns, the pigs, everything.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everything was destroyed, the entire infrastructure of the village, all the property. The cattle was driven away, and the tractors and other machinery was taken away and burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us who the victims were? What was their profession?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: The victims were mostly -- I don't want to insult anyone, but they were peasants, inhabitants of the village who lived there. For example, Zugic Koviljka, I think this old woman was 81 or 82 years old, and according to testimony of those closest to her, she -- her throat was slashed. And then Zugic Komljanin, who is missing, he was also an elderly person, he was over 70 years old. He is still missing. He was taken away from the village together with his son Trivko, and also Vlado Milinkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you please tell the Chamber this: Who are the three persons who conducted the investigation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: The investigation was carried out by Danilo Djeletovic, the then inspector of the public security centre in Sarajevo, which included the security station in Milici; then Zoran Durmic, that's me; and then also Dragan Savic, crime technician of the public security centre in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then in this last paragraph, can you please tell us the names the perpetrators. Who were these people who did this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: The commanders of units are mentioned here, the units that participated in this incident in this small village. So it is Zulfo Tursunovic, aka Tursun, and they acted from the direction of Zedanjsko. Then Ibrahim Ademovic, known as Cakura, his unit came from the direction of Djile. The village of Djile is neighbouring the village to Rupovo Brdo. They knew each other. Becir Mekanic came from the area of Stedra, to the north of the village. And then Fadil Turkovic, who was the former commander of the public security station from Vlasenica, his unit came from the direction of Kupusna. And let me just say that Kupusna lies in the direction of Zepa. According to some information or some statements of the people from his unit, it was learned that a month before that, he went to the area of Zepa, or Podzeplje to be more precise, and then he brought 20 well-trained soldiers. That was what he told them. And then also we have Mujo Bektic from Podgaj, this is the municipality of Srebrenica, because we -- the border between Milici and Srebrenica was there. His unit came from the direction of Zutica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you learn that on the same day at the same time, and how many similar incidents occurred before September 1992 in the area that was covered by your station, Milici and Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm not sure if we need that detailed evidence. Shall we move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell us how this reflected on the general situation in that area? What effect did it have on the Serbian people, on the fighters?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Well, how could it affect them? You can see that from these documents when they slashed the throat of their mother, killed their brother, take away the father who has not been found for the past 22 years. Then there were ambushes in Zutica where eight people were killed. In my translation, we got that this was the Boksit mine, but this was the village between Ravan. There were children, women, elderly people, and even though they were killed, explosives were thrown on that truck. The bodies were massacred. This was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Durmic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we accept -- can we tender this document now, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would still object on the basis of relevance to the charges in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, unless we're going to pretend that this was not a civil war, I don't see how the Prosecution can expect the trial to proceed with only attacks against Muslims and no evidence of what the Muslims did to the Serbs. I think it's highly relevant. It's not tu quoque evidence. It explains the events for which Mr. Karadzic is charged with planning, instigating and executing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, basically the document has been discussed at length with the witness, which is in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2949, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellencies. I don't have any questions for this witness at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Durmic, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony, as you have noted. You will now be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I can just have one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Durmic, the Milici branch station that you refer to became a public security station in early May 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that this was in early May. I think it was sometime in mid-May, because the public security station was formed in the area of the municipality of Milici pursuant to a decision by the minister of the interior. In any case, it was the month of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The chief of police, Rade Bjelanovic moved from being the chief the Vlasenica SJB to being the chief of the SJB Milici.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: No. I think you've not got it quite right. The late Mr. Bjelanovic was the chief of the public security station in Vlasenica. Part of that station, the Vlasenica station, we had the branch station in Milici. Later by forming the public security station in Milici, Mr. Milanovic [as interpreted] then transferred to become the chief of the public security station in Milici. In my interpretation I'm getting the security services centre, and I think that's a bigger branch.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last exchange between the accused and the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I think there's been -- I think there's been a mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, just please do not overlap. Do not overlap. Can we do without the exchange between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Durmic which was lost in their entirety because of overlapping?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I said was that in the transcript it was correct, but the oral interpretation was the CSB, and this is what confused the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So shall we start again. Yes, I leave it to you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Durmic, what -- what I said a moment ago was that the chief of the police, Rade Bjelanovic, moved from being the chief of the Vlasenica SJB, that is, the public security station, to become the chief of the SJB in Milici. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And there were approximately 40 police working at SJB Milici?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Well, we could never establish the exact number. It changed every day according to the situation, the organisation of the police, the reserves of the police. This is something that was approved through the department for Territorial Defence, the Territorial Defence Staff. So sometimes we would have 30 people, then we would have to let five go, then we would have 40, and we would release 10 for the needs of the army. So it was manned according to the needs and its duties in the area that it could serve, that it could carry out. This is for the needs of the people, if you understand me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And there was a Special Police Unit within the SJB at Milici, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was the commander of that Special Police Unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Again, we didn't understand each other. We did not have Special Police. Milici did not have Special Police. They had a public security station Milici, which as part of its composition had certain services, service of Milici dealing with public law and order, crime prevention. They had the criminal technical service. Then it had the administrative and legal affairs sector that dealt with different documents required by the citizens, driver's licences, passports, and so on. The special unit was at the level of the MUP. There wasn't one at the station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter number 24604, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting, can we ask to be told or notified about the documents that are going to be used in the cross-examination. We still have not received this notification.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. There was a miscommunication. It's coming right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Durmic, you see --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Durmic, you see in front of you a list of the Milici SJB employees for July 1995, and we see a list of -- of 37 names.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's quite small. Okay. Now it's been enlarged. Let me see. This is the list of those employed at the SJB at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. And -- and if you're looking at the names there, was -- were these policemen working in the SJB Milici in -- in the beginning of 1992 when the station, the SJB, was first formed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: No. No. I don't know if I could take six or seven of these people from this list who were there in 1992. I said earlier that it was all adapted to the situation. It would be increased or decreased. This is 1995, now, so the station was already functioning, had certain services. The number of policemen was engaged according to the existing classification.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, of course, the chief would be different because it's Rade Bjelanovic as opposed to Todor Boskovic, but if you go through the list of those names, could you just tell me the numbers of the people in the SJB who were working there in 1992? You don't have to say the names, you can just say the numbers.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Well, you just have to give me a little time to go over this. From what I remember, perhaps it was 15 or 16 people from this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. For example -- for example, number 6, do you recognise that name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And he was working there in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: He was working there from the 1980s already, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And number 27, for example?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: I think that he completed high school, perhaps that he started working in 1991, just before the war, and I think he was a ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Durmic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: He was an intern.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I seek to admit that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6126, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In your statement, you -- in paragraphs 30 to 32, you talk about the Zaklopaca incident, and you said that in paragraph 30, that on the day of the Zaklopaca massacre you were on the road section leading to the bauxite mine. How many were in this patrol with you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: There's an error again in the interpretation. I did not say at the crossroads, but I said that we were on the section. I meant a zone along the road of -- the regional road from Milici-Rudnik or Milici-Skelani where this road was captured by Muslim paramilitary units, because the territorials, the TO, tried to deblock that, and we from the police, of course, were supposed to place that under control, or we were supposed to secure that area that was freed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Durmic, my question was a simple one. How many people were on patrol with you that day when you said you were on the road section?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to explain to you that at the present wasn't a patrol but that it was basically the entire reserve force in the field. In the police station, there was only the duty service and perhaps a few people to secure the building and maybe two or three in the crime prevention department. The rest were up there on the road, because there was a threat of the road being blocked and the mine being taken over. So the entire area would be paralysed. It wasn't a simple patrol which would comprise, two, three, or up to five policemen, but this in turn included basically all of the members.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 00567.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Durmic, this is a daily -- or this is a report of -- a duty report from Milan Bacic, who was on duty on the 16th of May, 1992, where he says he took over duty at 7.00 a.m. in the morning, and he says here that all personnel were engaged in "ciscenje terena" operation.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: He probably believed it to be a mopping up operation. I'm trying to tell you that we were supposed to provide security along the road which had been deblocked by the territorials. So we assumed positions. It -- the road went through the valley in the direction of the mine and certain points needed to be secured, because people might be killed otherwise. Before the war they would stop vehicles and let people go on foot and so on and so forth. They would also stop trucks and cars.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter number 00568.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Durmic, again another report by Milan Bacic to the SJB commander, and again it says that on the 16th of May, the situation was regular and it was the same when he passed on the duty to the next person at 2300 hours, and again he said all personnel were engaged in a "ciscenje terena," cleaning operation. So again this -- and it says all personnel were engaged. It makes no reference to -- specifically to the area where you were, talking simply about all SJB personnel engaged on the ground in a cleaning up operation.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: I see here two different reports for the same date signed by the same person. The first report is different from this one in terms of sequence of reporting. In this report, it says that there were no parties to attend to during the duty shift, and in the other one the report is a different matter. So it's the same day, the same person, and two different reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that on the first one it does say no parties came during duty, and it also says that on the second report, just in a different order. The first report, 00567, talks about him taking over duty at 7.00 in the morning. The later report, 00568, refers to him passing on the duty at 2300 in the evening. So clearly it's two different reports written at two different times of the day, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm unaware of such practice of writing two reports when assuming duty and being relieved of duty. Usually reports are drafted at the end of one's duty, or perhaps the previous person submits a report on his duty before handing over. So it's usually at the end of the shift. I don't see why this person would draft two reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But you do know this Milan Bacic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: I barely knew him. I think they live somewhere in Sweden. He was with us for maybe a month and then he left. I didn't know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender those two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P6127 and P6128, respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Bacic -- Mr. Durmic, is it your evidence that it was the JNA who took part in the attack on the inhabitants of the village of Zaklopaca on the 16th of May, 1992, as it was passing through Milici? Yes -- yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: I can't say anything, because I didn't see it. I don't have any information. I can only presume, because on the 15th of May, there was the famous -- or infamous Tuzla column incident where the column was cut off. And there is a possibility that the tail, the end of the column was separated, and then they tried to turn back, and then there is the possibility --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Durmic, in relation to this incident, as you say, you -- it's your evidence that you weren't there and that you heard about this from someone else; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about it only in the evening when we returned from the field that I explained to you a moment ago. My workmate was killed, and later in the evening I went to visit his family, and many people were in attendance, in mourning. There was some rumour that something had taken place, but at that point in time I didn't pay much attention to it. That was the story that went around. That's the information I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Durmic. Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one topic, Your Excellency. Can we see P6126. It has been admitted a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Durmic, you made a distinction between employees and policemen. What does it mean? Who is a policemen, and who are the employees?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: No. No. There was a misunderstanding. The list of employees is from 1995. What I said was not that -- not all of these people were there in 1992. So by visual inspection, I said that maybe some 15 of them were there from the start in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Basically I wanted you to clear something up for us. Are all of these men policemen or are some of them administrative clerks?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DURMIC
utterances.text: No, no. At the top there is the chief, and then there is the secretary, the department for vehicle registration, for the issuing of IDs and other documents. There's the department in charge of cleaning. So many of these people are not authorised officials. They're not policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Durmic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, then that concludes your evidence, Mr. Durmic. I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the next witness is ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, he is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we could take an early break so that we could change seating, because Ms. Gustafson is leading the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She hasn't been in? Is she hiding? No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: She's coming. She's on her way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll have two 15 minutes' break before the lunch break. We'll see how it evolves. We'll take a break for 15 minutes now. Yes, just before that, yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't know what was more or less convenient, Mr. President, but I'm sure Ms. Gustafson is on her way. If you just want to take a couple minutes, I'm sure we could set up. I don't want to create any trouble for the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's what I wanted too but -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sure it'll be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This time we'll take a 15-minute break. We'll resume at 10.32 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Veselinovic. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Veselinovic.

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to remind us both to speak slowly and to put pauses between your question -- between our questions and answers so as to have everything reflected in the transcript. Did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D7230 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The statement you see on the screen, is it the one you gave to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read it and signed it?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've read it and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the last page, please, in order to see the signature and identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that it is your signature?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the statement accurately and entirely convey what you shared with the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers be essentially the same as we can find them in the statement?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I seek to tender the 92 ter package, and I will have to lead a few documents live with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're tendering eight associated exhibits, and we would ask that each of them be added to the 65 ter list as we didn't have -- had not interviewed the witness at the time we prepared that list. The first one is 1D12044. The second, 1D12045. The third, 1D12046. The fourth, 1D048. The fifth, 1D12049. The sixth, 1D12053. The seventh, 1D12054. And the eighth, 1D12055.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. If I understand correctly, neither of the videos are being tendered, so we had an objection to one of the videos, but I understand from what was just said that the videos aren't being tendered. I understand 1D12045 and 1D12054 are now the only exhibits being tendered for which there is no translation, and those are the ones as we indicated in our e-mail yesterday that should be led live. Other than that there are no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: When I checked this morning there were translations for those two, but if the Chamber hasn't had a chance to look at them we can pass them, but there were translations this morning --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I should clarify. There were -- I agree there are translations but the translations that are in e-court are translations of the previous documents that were at least in large part illegible. So the translations now don't match the contents of the newly provided documents. So there is still a translation issue for those two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Very well. If those two documents are to be led live, we'll admit the Rule 92 ter statement as well as other six associated exhibits. We will give the number for the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D2950, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we give the numbers for the other associated exhibits in lump sum from -- six numbers altogether.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Those will be Exhibits D2951 through to Exhibit D2956 respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. In the order of the Rule 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to read out a summary of Mr. Veselinovic's statement in the English language. [In English] Sveto Veselinovic was the president of the SDS Municipal Board in Rogatica from 1990, when it was founded, to March 1992. After the first multi-party elections, he was elected a member of the municipal Executive Committee. Just before the war, he was chief of the municipal public revenue administration. In May 1992, he became a member of the Crisis Staff in Rogatica. In September 1992, he was appointed head of income administration by the president of the Executive Committee of Rogatica. He remained in that position until the end of 1993, when he moved to the Ministry of Trade to become a republic financial inspector. Sveto Veselinovic assisted with the preparations for the founding assembly of the SDS in Rogatica municipality, which was also attended by representatives of the SDA Muslim party. Up until the second half of the 1991, the political situation in BH was cordial, co-operation was encouraged, and the break-up of Yugoslavia and one-track policies criticised. Following the multi-party elections, the departments in local government and leading functions in public institutions were divided up very quickly. However, it became clear to Sveto Veselinovic that the SDA abandoned its declared policy and began to focus their activities on the secession of B and H from Yugoslavia. The first problem in Rogatica began when the division of functions agreed on 4th of January, 1991, was to be implemented because for certain functions the approval of the republican organs was necessary. This meant that agreements reached in the municipality were abandoned. At this the Serbs organised a protest on the square near the municipal building. The SDA assisted in resolving this matter. However, under pressure from the SDA central office the Rogatica SDA leadership became less cooperative and changed their position, adopting the policy for the creation of a unitary independent Bosnia. Sveto Veselinovic considers that the media placed themselves in the service of the SDA Muslim party, and therefore the SDS had less room to express their views publicly. Therefore, announcements were made in an attempt to inform the public that the Muslim authorities were departing from their mandate and failing to implement the policies they initially promoted. Sveto Veselinovic considers that tension in Rogatica municipality reached its climax during the mobilisation of the JNA unit on 30th of June, 1991. A number of Muslims boycotted the mobilisation, and for those that did not boycott the SDA from Rogatica -- the SDA from Rogatica sent buses to the place where the unit had been mobilised and returned all the Muslims home. To fill the gap left by the Muslims, Serbs were called up to preserve the common state. After this, the Muslims attacked the JNA even more, saying it was a mono-ethnic army. However, Sveto Veselinovic considers that this was caused by the SDA themselves. Throughout 1991, the tensions grew and the Muslims were being armed en masse. Due to his position, Sveto Veselinovic had contact with a number of Muslims, and on one occasion, Hasan Sehic showed him a pistol that he had received as a member of the SDA Main Board. He told Sveto Veselinovic that other members had also received these pistols. Due to the growing mistrust, villages -- village guards were organised in late 1991, and Sveto Veselinovic was aware that Muslims had also organised similar guards. The SDS made many efforts to avoid clashes, and therefore they agreed to divide the municipality to prevent the large-scale conflicts. However, in March 1992, a Serbian home was attacked. Sveto Veselinovic suspected it was done to intimidate the Serbian people. This sparked the locals to form a Territorial Defence to protect against Muslim attacks. In order to preserve peace and involve as many people as possible, a letter was sent out to prominent people who held various offices, inviting them to join the Crisis Staff. The staff was a large body whose main tasks were to negotiate on the delineation of the municipality's territory and the division of power. Further, during the war, the work of the SDS was frozen, and the party did not engage in any activities until just before the end of the war. The murder of the Serb Drazenko Mihajlovic, a Serb policeman, in May 1992, suspended all efforts regarding any further negotiations on securing peace. After this incident, larger-scale conflicts broke out and refugees appeared on both sides. On the 30th of May, 1992, a commission was formed to accommodate and help the refugees. The refugees were accommodated in a controlled and organised manner in abandoned Muslim and Serb apartments and houses. Notices were visibly placed on all the doors stating that moving in without the commission's authorisation or decision was prohibited. At this time, due to the growing insecurity in the town and shooting in the streets, both Serbs and Muslims left the town and moved to its suburbs and further away. Transport was organised for Serbian families and at the same time, more refugees were arriving. Sveto Veselinovic was aware that a number of Serbs and Muslims threatened by danger in the town moved into a building of the secondary school centre. From there they were sent to their desired locations. When Sveto Veselinovic entered Rogatica after fighting had occurred and was shocked by what he saw as the town had been entirely devastated, many Serbian houses and apartments had been torched and reduced to their foundations. Sveto Veselinovic remembers that Dr. Karadzic was in Rogatica on 2nd of August, 1991, during an important religious holiday and stayed one night because he was on a trip to Uzice in Serbia. He also remembers that next visit to Rogatica was in autumn 1993, when Karadzic visited the leadership. [Interpretation] That will be the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to put to you a few questions about the documents that you kindly made available to us. First of all, shall I address you as Dr. Veselinovic, because you have a Ph.D., don't you?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In one of the paragraphs here, you dealt with the division of power just after the elections.

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D12040 is the document I would like to call up in e-court. 1D12040.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what is this record? What is the subject matter?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: This is the record from the meeting of commissions for inter-party co-operation between the Serbian Democratic Party and the Party of Democratic Action concerning the division of power in Rogatica municipality. This record lists exhaustively all the leading positions that were to be divided up between two parties who had the elections, and at the end we find the signatures of all those who attended the meeting, namely, seven members of the SDS and seven members of the SDA. The record was done on the 4th of January, 1991, and we drafted it in less than two hours. So everything was very expeditiously agreed in this municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in these talks?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm one of the signatories.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does this last sentence mean?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: The last sentence says that 27 mandates were allocated to the SDA in this division. I can't see the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll see it on the next page. And their mandates included president of the municipality as the most senior position.

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Again, last sentence.

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian Democratic Party got a total of 21 mandates in line with the structure of the votes won we divided the power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was the most important position for the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Chairman of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the last page, please. Yes, last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are these the participants in the talks?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the signatures. On the left are those from the SDA. At the very bottom is the signature of the president of their party. And on the right-hand side we see the signatures of the participants from the Serbian Democratic Party, and at the bottom is my signature as president of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be MFI'd, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI'd D2957, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned it in the statement, but can you tell us, how did the first disagreements arise erasing this idyll from just after the elections?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: The first disagreements broke out after -- about the implementation of this agreement concerning certain positions. Approval from republic organs had to be obtained, such as the position of chief of the police station and the commander of the police station in Rogatica. The ministry of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina sent their approval for a Muslim to be appointed chief of the police station, but they did not send approval for a Serb to be appointed commander of the police station. That is why we organised the protest before the building of the Municipal Assembly where I read out our demand that our representative be appointed to his post as well. And the local Muslims did not have any problem with our protest. Even our Muslim friend who worked for the MUP promised his help, wrote directly to the republic MUP and ensured that both appointments were approved. This was covered by the media, and I believe on the 16th of May, 1991, a story appeared in the newspaper "Oslobodjenje."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything in the developments at the level of Yugoslavia that perhaps contributed to rising tensions?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. As things got more and more complicated at the level of Yugoslavia, the local Muslims appeared less and less cooperative, adhered less and less to the agreements we had reached, and began obeying instructions from the SDA head office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D12047, please. 1D12047.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a press release you made on behalf of the Regional Board of SDS for Romanija, dated 11 May 1991. Can you tell us what is the gist of this press release?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: The events unfolding on the territory of Yugoslavia, including Bosnia and Herzegovina, created an increasing rift between the Muslim people and the Serbian people and stoked hatred on the part of Muslims and Croats towards Serbs. This is about tying the Croatian and Muslim flags into an unbreakable knot, stopping the JNA column at Siroki Brijeg and preventing them from carrying out their military drills. This also contains a critique of Sarajevo media who were more and more biased in favour of Muslims, and information that the Serbs tried to put out in the media was stopped, and even this press release could not be placed in their media. We could only publish it in our local media and the local radio Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be MFI'd, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI 2958, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were also a member of the Crisis Staff in Rogatica municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that a one-party Crisis Staff or was it a Crisis Staff that was a body of authority?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, we created a Crisis Staff within the party that was intended to inform our central party authorities about all that was going on in our municipality. However, when problems escalated to such an extent that we, representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party, became unable to deal with them on our own, or better to say we did not have the mandate from the SDS leadership to take our people to war, we had to invite all the prominent Serbs in Rogatica who were not SDS members but had been in leading positions in business, in the economy, et cetera, inviting them to join a new Crisis Staff of Rogatica that would not be a mono-party unit but would be made up of prominent people from all over Rogatica. Such a staff was indeed established on the 8th of April, 1992, and Mr. Milorad Sokolovic was appointed chairman of this Crisis Staff of which I was a member.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D12050, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Veselinovic, were you elected immediately or a bit later?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, in your introduction, you mentioned that two grenades were thrown at a Serb house in Borike. That house belonged to Rajko Kusic, a member of our SDS. When his house was bombed, he withdrew to Borike. He linked up the, until then, disorganised local guards, and he formed the Territorial Defence under the law that said that a local commune had the right to form its own Territorial Defence in case of an immediate threat of war. Rajko Kusic and I continued to work for preserving peace with the Muslim side. It was our hope that we will achieve peace, because Izetbegovic had signed the Cutileiro Plan, otherwise known as the Lisbon Agreement, but when Alija Izetbegovic withdrew his signature, the Territorial Defence at Borike believed that further negotiations were pointless. They had information that Muslims were very hastily preparing for war and might attack at any minute. That attack would involve liquidating all prominent Serbs in the municipality in one night. Mr. Kusic said he did not want to bear responsibility if that happened, if all the Serbs were killed, and he said that we had to attack them first. I, Tomislav Batinic, and Mr. Ujic did not agree. We thought that peace had no alternative and that we had no mandate to take the Serbian people to war. That evening, the three of us resigned on all our positions in the Serb Democratic Party. The next day I spoke to Kusic, I proposed to him to invite all the Serbs from the territory of the municipality, involve them in our joint work and form a new Crisis Staff at the level of the municipality. Kusic agreed. The next day I invited all those people, talked to them. They agreed, but they required that their appointments be verified by some authority. We called up the -- we convened the Municipal Board of the party, and their appointments were verified. I personally was not quite happy, though. In order to prove to myself and to the Serbian people that I did not care for a high position at any cost, and I don't want to see other people get killed under my bad command, I myself put on a uniform and joined a JNA unit that had been formed in -- sorry, a Territorial Defence unit that had been formed at Sjemec.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I didn't want you to repeat what you said in the statement. I'm just asking about this new Crisis Staff after your resignations. On the 21st of May, as we see here, you were mobilised onto the Crisis Staff. Can you read this out, when you were mobilised? You cannot on the screen but I can see it on paper. Who signed this and from what party is this person?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I received a summons when I was in the unit of the JNA. I received a summons that I was mobilised and deployed to the Crisis Staff and that I should immediately report to the Crisis Staff. The signature of the decision that I was issued is that of the president of the Crisis Staff, Mile Sokolovic, who was appointed on the 8th of April as president of the Crisis Staff. He's not from the Serbian Democratic Party. I think he's from the Democratic Alliance, that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Line 20, page 40, instead of "Rajko Kusic and myself continued, we remained in Rogatica," I think that you said that it was you and Mile Ujic and Tomislav Batinic who stayed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please. I would like it MFI'd, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I just note that there is a more legible version of this document that we were provided, but it appears that that more legible version is not in e-court yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Together with English translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There is no English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. If we have more legible one, could you replace it later. Yes. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2959, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you dealing with any other aspects of the crisis or problems in the Rogatica municipality? Were you in any ad hoc bodies besides your regular work duties?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: My specific task in the Crisis Staff was initially to deal with organisation, reception, and accommodation of refugees. After Rogatica was liberated, I was charged with going into the town with a group of retired carpenters to protect the town from break-ins and robberies, which means that I entered the town first immediately after the liberators, and since I had a camera with me, I recorded the situation as I found it in that town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the refugees, could we look at 1D12051, please, in e-court. 12051.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: This document was issued by the Crisis Staff. It's a decision on forming a commission for refugees and for resolving the matter of their accommodation. I was the president of that commission, and it was signed by the president of the Crisis Staff, Mile Sokolovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2960, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you later appointed to a leadership post in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: When there was no longer any need for the Crisis Staff, the Executive Board was formed and I became a member of the Executive Board, and my specific assignment was to be the secretary of the Secretariat for General Administration and for the finance administration or revenue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 12054 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Veselinovic, what is this document about?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document that was issued by the Executive Board of the municipality of Rogatica. It is a decision on assignment to work duty where I am assigned to work in the Executive Board of the municipality of Rogatica, and I was assigned to the Executive Board and also acting director of the revenue administration, and it was signed --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where do you know that this was the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: It states: "On the basis of Article 7, item 2 of the regulation or organising and executing work duty Official Gazette of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," then it says, "the president of the Executive Board adopts the following decision."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2961, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Other than the commission for the accommodation of refugees, was there any other commission charged with assisting the refugees, and did you play any role in any commission if there was such a commission?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: The first document that you showed me was the decision appointing me as the president of the commission, which was issued before we received the Official Gazette notifying us about the adoption of the Law on Refugees. Then there was a document issued pursuant to the new law as well as a document appointing me commissioner for refugees for direct co-operation and contacts with the republican commissioner for refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D12052, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is this document? Who issued it?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: This document was issued by the Serbian municipality of Rogatica, Executive Board. It's a decision on forming a commission for assistance to refugees. Again I was appointed president of that commission. It's a new body that issued a new decision in accordance with the law as published in the Official Gazette of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina, number 792, the Executive Board of the Serbian municipality of Rogatica, and it had to do with assisting refugees. It was signed by the president, Milorad Sokolovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2962, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Veselinovic, you mentioned today in your testimony, as well as in your statement, in paragraph 18, that you were the first one to enter Rogatica after it was liberated. When did you enter Rogatica, and under whose control was it before that or up until then?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
