utterances.text: The centre of the town was under the control of the Muslim forces. After combat and after Rogatica was freed by Serbian forces - I don't know the exact date when it was finally liberated, but it was sometime in July - as member of these commissions and the Presidency entrusted with care for refugees and security and safety of abandoned property on behalf of the Crisis Staff or the Executive Board at the time, I entered the town intending to record how I found it and to form a group in order to protect the abandoned properties from robberies and theft. So this was maybe some five or six days after the final liberation when units of the Serbian Army had already withdrawn from Rogatica, leaving just some individual guards. And the population was still not permitted to enter the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to give us your comments on the video footage that you made at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D7229, please, and then I will give you the counter number. So 1D7229, please. The first clip is from 1 minute 20 seconds to 1 minute 37 seconds. That's the first clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And whenever you think it's appropriate, could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what it is that we are seeing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we play the footage, please, from 1:20 to 1:37, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this footage we're going to see what the destroyed town looks like, broken shop windows, the goods in the shops looted, burned-out storefronts, the town completely destroyed and devastated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 12:29 to 12:34, please. That would be the timer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see a knocked-down and burned house belonging to my wife's family. Please take note of the grass around the house, meaning that the burning is not something that was a result of the combat, but it was something that occurred a month before that, meaning that the house was torched immediately after the Serbs left it, left the inner city, the centre. All the houses belonging to Serbs and a good part of the apartments belonging to them were burned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 16:32 up to 17:00. 16:32 to 17:00, please. This is the next clip.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we see in this footage is an abandoned machine-gun nest abandoned of the Muslim forces abandoned when they left the town. This machine-gun nest is located in the area of the upper town on top of a building and it faced the nearby local hill where the Serbian settlements were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whose machine-gun nest is it? It's not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: It's a Muslim machine-gun nest at the top of a building, and they abandoned it when they were pulling out. They were probably withdrawing very quickly, and it was difficult for them to take the machine-gun down from the top of the building to take it with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what do you see on these roofs that we see in front of the building, this first roof, the closest one?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can see the broken roof tiles, partially destroyed roofs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what were the buildings that they used or facilities in order to place machine-gun nests there?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Besides this one, there is another one that we're going to see. They used predominantly tall buildings, tall positions from where they could see the entire town, the lower and upper parts of the town where the Serbs were. And we can include their mosques and the minarets of the mosques among those tall buildings from which sniper action was also recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 19:26 to 20:15 on the counter. 19:26 to 20:15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the centre of town. The building that you see is where my brother Lazar had his apartment. There were two other apartments belonging to two Serbs, Ljubo Coric and Radenko Perisic. All those apartments were burned. What you are seeing right now is a hotel. That was also torched. It was also set on fire as they were withdrawing. And then in the next shot we can see sandbags. This is probably another machine-gun nest. No weapons were found here, but what you cannot see on the footage is that on the left-hand side is the municipal building and the building of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the last clip, please, from 21:34 to 22:10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I may ask you to explain to us what we are seeing here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the mosque burned down in the town. I don't know how it burned down, but I would like you to look at the next shot. Only 30 metres away from the mosque is their second machine-gun nest. Probably our artillery in an attempt to neutralise this machine-gun nest could have made an error and have hit the mosque. Just a little bit earlier, I did mention that there was talk of them also having snipers on top of their mosques too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender these clips into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit those clips that we saw in one number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2963, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please look at 1D7228, please, from 6:13 to 7:32, please. 06 -- actually, 00:03 to 53. Actually, 00 to 3:53. From the very beginning, running up to 3:53.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This footage shows the refugees from Gorazde who were expelled on the 27th of August, 1992, by Muslims from their hearths. A column of these refugees came up against a Muslim ambush in which 25 of them were killed and more than 80 wounded. I would like to draw your attention to the fact that none of these people have weapons. This means that these were exclusively civilians, men, women, children, who were attacked by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many of them arrived from Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. What I do know is that a bit less than 1.000 of them remained in Rogatica, because I could see that from my lists of refugees. Most of them, though, the very next day went to Serbia via Vlasenica and Zvornik. That evening, a member of the Presidency, Ms. Biljana Plavsic, arrived. She spoke with them and tried to have them stay in Rogatica, promising that they would be accommodated in empty houses and flats. However, most of them still went to Serbia via Vlasenica and Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Veselinovic, can you tell us what did it all mean for the municipality? In other words, how successful was the municipality in dealing with the situation given the numbers of destroyed homes and the lack of housing units?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Many of those refugees who arrived in such a short time put an end to our attempts to prevent the destruction of any abandoned properties. It wasn't only them but also refugees from our municipalities who entered such premises and found accommodation there. They also entered many houses unlawfully, taking away things that were -- they needed for normal life like bed linen and different items. That was because they had only the several items left which they could fit into the trunks of their cars as they were leaving their homes. You can see the women and children here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What are the age groups of these people?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: We can see in the footage that there are very small children as well as the elderly who are over 80 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go to 06:13 to 07:32.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This footage shows how we tried to protect the housing units. We see the piece of paper that was placed on the door prohibiting entry. However, the situation was simply such that we could not follow through on what we had envisaged, and many buildings and flats were entered and people took away whatever they needed such as clothing items, footwear, et cetera. Of course, those who primarily wanted to loot also found fruitful ground. You can see what an apartment looks like after this turmoil in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was left behind by our refugees; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when we were locking apartments, they were mostly tidy. This means that what we can see here was left behind by not only our refugees but also different kinds of dogs of war, if I can call them that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender these few excerpts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We have no objection the latter clip. It appears to have some relevance. The first clip depicting the gathering of Serbs from Gorazde and Rogatica doesn't appear to have any relevance to the charges in this case, and we object on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think the testimony couldn't be understood without it, and it's clearly relevant because it shows the arrival of all the refugees.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I'd like to make a correction. These Serbs were not from Rogatica. These were the Serbs from Rogatica who arrived in -- these were the Serbs from Gorazde who arrived in Rogatica who had been ambushed, and it was a wholly new problem for the municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could see the registration plates on the cars indicating that they arrived from Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We heard the evidence. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2964, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions for Dr. Veselinovic at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic, as you have noted, most of your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, but before we're doing so we'll have a short break. But there are a couple of matters I'd like to deal with, i.e., I'd like to issue two oral rulings. First thing, the Chamber is seized of the accused's request for state representative to be present in the courtroom with respect to Ambassador Jose Cutileiro which was filed on the 4th of February, 2013, in which the accused submits that Ambassador Cutileiro requested that two representatives of the government of Portugal be present in the courtroom during his testimony. After having reviewed the information contained in the correspondence filed by the accused on the 15th of February, 2013, the Chamber is satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to allow the two Portuguese representatives to be present in the courtroom during Ambassador Cutileiro's testimony. Accordingly, the Chamber grants the request. In addition, the Chamber requests the Registry to provide the transcript of this ruling to Portugal. Next is related to the Prosecution's request for leave to reply to Karadzic's response to Prosecution motion to exclude Vasiljevic evidence. Since the Chamber finds that it would be in the interests of justice, the Chamber hereby allows the -- grants the request. We'll have a short break for 15 minutes and resume at 5 to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Veselinovic.

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, it's clear from your evidence that you were the president -- the first president of the SDS in Rogatica. Until when exactly, to the best of your recollection, did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 25th of March, I submitted my resignation to all positions in the party and municipality. However, the Municipal Assembly, which sat on the 8th of April, when the Crisis Staff was established, did not accept my resignation in entirety but, actually, they froze my status. As the war broke out, the party no longer functioned properly from the level of the republic down, and following that, I was engaged solely in such activities as issued to me by the president of the Crisis Staff. Perhaps sometime in 1994, party life developed again, and there were elections for president. In 1998, I was again in that position for a mandate of about four years, which was after the war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correction for the transcript. In line 12, the witness said that from the republican level party life was put on hold as well. That's not what found its way in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it was there, but let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You said that you submitted your resignation from all your positions in the party on the 25th of March, which I understand was 1992, and then from your evidence earlier this morning, it was sometime after that that you joined a TO unit. Do you remember when exactly you joined the TO unit?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I did not join a TO unit. I joined a JNA unit. It was a brigade which was located at Han Pijesak. One of its units, its battalion, was in Rogatica. I joined the unit two or three days following my resignation. In other words, I held a meeting with the Serbs from Rogatica municipality, with prominent members of the leadership past and present, I agreed on their participation in the work of the Crisis Staff and left only to join the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So that was sometime towards the end of March, and then you also in your evidence earlier said that, if I understand correctly, while you were in this JNA unit, you were then summoned and mobilised to work at the Crisis Staff, and you were shown a document indicating that mobilisation, and it had a mobilisation date of the 21st of May, 1992. And that's MFI D2959. So is it correct on the 21st of May or thereabouts you left the JNA unit and began working for the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I think I left the unit even before that. The decision arrived later for organisational reasons. The unit I was in following my departure went in the direction of Sarajevo, to the area of Grbavica to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the Chamber's heard evidence that that unit went to the area of Grbavica at the beginning of May. So do you think you left your JNA unit sometime around the beginning of May or before?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Before the unit went to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So we can agree, then, that you were in this -- for the -- in 1992, you were only a member of this JNA unit for a brief period of time between sometime in late March and sometime in early May. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: As of early April until late May.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to move on to another topic which relates to paragraph 21 of your statement, where it says that you were shown the statement of a Muslim who listed the types of weapons he had in his village. The prior version of your statement that we received identified this statement as that of Fehim Kapo from Kramer Selo. And as you note in your statement, Mr. Kapo had stated that they had 40 automatic rifles, some hunting rifles and some explosives in the village. And you say, "This indicates that all the other villages were similarly armed," and then you go on to complain about "evidence," and you put that term in quotes in your statement, that the Muslims disseminated in the media about Serbs arming and that they were under threat as result because they did not have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 1D07560, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, I take it from your statement that you were shown this statement of Mr. Kapo's by the Defence investigators, and they were you were asked to draw some conclusions about the general level of arming by the Muslims based on that statement. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: This statement only confirms what we knew. If in a village of 57 households and 222 inhabitants -- I have it noted down in my notebooks, because I took part in the 1991 census. This witness said himself that they had 40 automatic rifles, some hunting rifles, and some explosive ordnance. If we take that data, that there were 40 automatic rifles for 50 households and every household had around four members, two of which were children and the wife and husband, it means that any able -- any and every able-bodied man had an automatic rifle in a village which was not of strategic importance for the Muslims. If you take that, you can only imagine how well armed they were in the town itself and other villages. We had known that before, and I mentioned in my statement, that as the director of the public revenue administration, I was in contact with many Muslims, because I was in charge of assessing taxes based on movable and immovable property, taxes levied on economic activity for companies and entrepreneurs. It means, in other words, that I was aware of the information pertaining to every taxpayer in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I interrupted you because we've moved away from the direct question that I'd asked you, and I'd ask you to please focus on the precise question I'm asking and try to limit your answers to respond just to that precise question, and I will try to keep my questions precise. Now, I'd like to direct your attention to a passage in this statement beginning about halfway down the first paragraph, and it says: "Having followed the developments in April 1992 and the preparations on the part of the former JNA, which was joined by the local Serbian population, we, the inhabitants of the village, organised village guards. We would observe them deploy weapons and artillery pieces around our village and train their barrels on our village, allegedly afraid of us being numerous and armed. The weapons and artillery pieces deployed included four tanks, two armoured personnel carriers, an unidentified number of cannons and mortars and other small arms." And then Mr. Kapo goes on to identify Mr. Boban Jesic and Rajko Kusic as the commanders in the area. And in the next page in the English, he says: "In contrast to them, we had around 40 submachine-guns and a number of hunting rifles and explosive devices." So it's clear, as you indicate in your statement, that Mr. Kapo said that the Muslims of Kramer Selo had 40 automatic weapons and hunting rifles and some explosive devices, but it's also clear that the Muslims of Kramer Selo were nevertheless under threat from a far more powerful array of Serb weapons deployed around their villages, namely, tanks, APCs, cannons, and mortars. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: That is not right. A moment ago you said yourself that there was a JNA unit which for a period was stationed in Sjemec and then went to Sarajevo. They were fully equipped in terms of weaponry. Our TO was armed in a similar way as the Muslims. In other words, with infantry weapons. The TO did not have any tanks or any heavy weapons. According to military speciality, all those who could man and service tanks and heavy weapons joined the unit which went to Sarajevo. The TO comprised elderly men as well as younger men who perhaps had not served their military service at the time. This witness's statement on the type of weapons is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber has received evidence from Mr. Ujic, who was a witness for the Defence and who actually co-ordinated artillery for the Rogatica Brigade, that at some point in time there was artillery surrounding this village because he testified to personally commanding -- or personally co-ordinating, sorry, the shelling attack of Kramer Selo, an attack that caused the population to flee and resulted in the wounding of some children by shrapnel. And I refer to transcript pages 33466 to 33467. Were you unaware of the fact that this village was ultimately shelled and the population fled?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the quote and time that Ujic's statement refers to? Was the JNA still there or -- can we have a reference for the quote?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you check the page numbers Ms. Gustafson referred to? Please come back after checking in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In any event, Your Honours, the question was framed that at some point in time there was artillery surrounding the village, so I think the question is fair regardless of the time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the witness will be able to deal with this. Can you answer the question, Mr. Veselinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps that question should be put to Mr. Mile Ujic again to clarify what period it concerns. Finally, he took part in those operations. I don't know what units they acted in co-ordination with them. At the time, I was at the Crisis Staff, and I wasn't familiar with it. The army was under no obligation to inform us of their plans and operations, as well as with the kind of weapons they had at their disposal to attack. It is my subjective opinion that such unit, knowing the people who remained in the area and who were not any military experts -- well, Mile perhaps was the only military officer. As a member of the Executive Board and the Crisis Staff, he remained in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And at paragraph 11 of your statement, you assert that the Muslims were being armed en masse, and as support for that assertion you explain how you learned that some SDA members in Rogatica had received pistols. You don't say anything in your statement about Serb arming. However, the Chamber heard extensive and detailed evidence from Asim Dzambasovic, who was the Chief of Staff of the 216th Brigade of the JNA, regarding JNA arming of Serbs in Rogatica in the period leading up to the war. And I refer to P2828, paragraphs 41 to 54. And that evidence included his diary entry for the 29th of January, 1992, where he stated: "Despite the irrefutable arguments, the commander does not want to undertake measures against the ones who are stealing the weapons. He is encouraging distribution of weapons and is giving them away by his own free will. Superior command Colonel Gagovic and Djurdjevac second this silently." Now, were you aware of these concerns expressed at the level of the brigade command regarding the arming of Serbs by the JNA in Rogatica supported by the brigade and corps command?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army did not arm Serbs in Rogatica. The JNA supplied weapons to Serbs who joined the JNA. Otherwise, there was no need for them to give anyone any weapons. When the Muslims decided to ignore mobilisation call-ups and stopped joining the JNA, the JNA became mostly Serbs, but otherwise the army provided weapons only to new conscripts. The JNA did not need to supply weapons to Serbs. The Serbs were anxious to keep the JNA as a force keeping their state together. So what this witness said in his evidence is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. In regard to the mobilisation you just referred to, I'd like to go to -- I believe it's D2953. It's an associated exhibit admitted this morning. Mr. Veselinovic, you referred in your statement in several places to your efforts to preserve peace, and you reiterated that in your evidence this morning. And this is a "Politika" article from July 1991 that you described in your statement at paragraph 14, and it relates to the JNA mobilisation that the Chamber's heard evidence occurred in June of 1991. And in the second paragraph it states that the Serbs responded -- or the Serbs left en masse for the front, and that's a claim you also make in paragraph 10. And in the article you complain that only 10 per cent of the Muslim reservists who responded to the mobilisation went to Banja Luka, whereas the Serbs responded in the largest numbers, and you state that this left the Serbian villages deserted. Now, again, Mr. Dzambasovic, who at the time was -- participated in implementing this mobilisation and who went to Banja Luka with the conscripts, gave evidence that there was a general failure by both Serbs and Muslims to respond to this mobilisation. And then there was a further mass refusal by the soldiers to go to Banja Luka because they were afraid of being sent to Vukovar and getting killed. And as a result, of the 4.000 soldiers in the brigade at the time, only about 800 of any ethnicity went to the front. And that's at Exhibit P2828, paragraphs 14 to 26. So the basic premise of this article that the Serbs responded en masse to this mobilisation is -- leaving the elderly, children, and female Serbs vulnerable to Muslim attacks, is at best a major exaggeration because, in fact, only about 1 in 5 brigade soldiers of any ethnicity went to the front. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: That is not so. We heard this morning that just a few Muslims responded to the mobilisation call-up who went back very quickly because the SDA had sent buses to fetch them in Banja Luka and bring them back. Some people responded, but only thanks to our efforts and agitation, because they had not even received the call-up papers because the SDA blocked normal, regular mobilisation because they hid the military papers. The entire unit was not even planned to go to Banja Luka, the unit made up of Serbs. But when the Muslims started ignoring the mobilisation call-ups, the fear became real. If the Serb villages are empty, if there are not enough able-bodied men to protect them and the Muslims -- the Muslim men were still there because they had not joined the army, we were thinking why are they organising themselves if they are not joining the army? You cannot imagine it, but at that time refusing the call-up meant a long prison sentence, because you were treated like an enemy of the state. So you could only do that wishing that the unit would be -- fall apart, that the state would fall apart and you would never be held responsible, and that meant in turn that you are doing everything to destroy that state. So our fears were justified. We believed the Muslim objective was to destroy the state, and that's why they were trying to prevent even the Serbs from staying within the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. It's clear your evidence is that this failure to respond to the mobilisation was part of a plot to destroy the state. And in this article you are quoted as saying: "We have a message for all those who are preparing dirty war plans, that the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina are ready and that 1941 will never be repeated." Your reference to 1941 here is an evocation of the mass murder and persecution of Serbs during World War II, an event I suspect you would probably characterize as a genocide; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1941, the Serb people were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'd just like you to keep your answers as precise as possible. And -- and --

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: My answer is yes, the Serb people were destroyed in 1941, but our readiness -- I did not finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I had just asked for you to confirm that you -- what you were referring to regarding the events of 1941. I think your answer's clear. And then when you said, "We have a message for all those who are preparing dirty war plans, the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina are ready and that 1941 will never be repeated," you were warning that the Muslims are preparing war plans that involve the destruction of the Serb people akin to what happened in 1941, and that the Serbs are ready to use force in the face of this Muslim threat; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not right. I didn't say that the Serbs were ready to use force. I said this they were ready to stop it from happening again. They would not be sitting in their houses waiting to be rounded up, taken to camps and killed. They were ready to join the JNA, the legitimate army, and defend the state in which they had lived, in which they were born, and they wanted to continue living in. I didn't say that they were ready to respond with force and kill. That's not written there. Please do not put words in my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: By disseminating this warning that the Muslims are planning mass murder, as you call it, destruction of the Serb people, and saying that the Serbs are ready to respond to that threat, such a statement coming from the head of the SDS in Rogatica in July 1991, that could only have added to the fears and ethnic tensions at the time. Don't you agree?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't agree. That's not so. It was a warning to those Serbs who hadn't yet woken up, who were still believing in brotherhood and unity. It was a warning to them that we could be tricked again. We were putting to them real facts that they could not learn from BH media. Serbs had no access to the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's why I approached the daily "Politika" that was published and printed in Belgrade and was still widely read in our region and enjoyed trust.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 14 of your statement - I'm moving on now to another topic - you state that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say something? Concerning that intervention on pages 33466 and 467, I would appreciate it if Ms. Gustafson quoted properly rather than ascribing part of her question to Mr. Mile Ujic. He did not say that he had taken part in the attack that caused the population to flee. We would not be allowed to do this, misrepresenting one witness's statement to another witness. He said -- you can look up, for instance, 33467. Let's rewind. "The point of our offer was you hand over your weapons, you live peacefully and normally. If there is fire coming from a village, it's not a village any more. It's a military target, a legitimate military target, especially after the killings that happened on that road."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we proceed or would you like to respond, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would like to proceed. I will look back again at the transcript reference and respond in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic, on -- at paragraph 14 of your statement, you say: "On the 22nd of May, the Muslims were finally ready for the war and carried out an attack on the Serbs. " Now I take it you were not involved in planning or implementing any military activities in Rogatica at this time in late May; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, that Serb policeman Mihajlovic Drazenko was killed and the chairman of our Crisis Staff, Mile Sokolovic, called upon the opposite side to let us recover the body of that policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: My question was whether you were involved in planning or implementing any military activities in Rogatica at this time, late May. If you could please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm going to put it to you that your evidence about the Muslims attacking the Serbs on the 22nd of May is completely untrue. The Serbs attacked the Muslims of Rogatica on the 22nd of May by shelling parts of the town in Muslim-populated villages and carrying out an infantry attack on parts of the town. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I know for a fact that the first person killed in Rogatica was Drazenko Mihajlovic, and he was killed in May. Whether it was the 22nd of May, I can't say, but the killing of Drazenko Mihajlovic was the first Serb killed. You interrupted me a moment ago when I was saying the president of our Crisis Staff contacted the Muslim side, asking them to approve that we recover the body and bury him, and they answered, "When we kill another 10, then we will let you have all the bodies." That's what I learnt from our president, and that was our last telephone contact with them. After that, all-out war began. Now, what was attacked, in what sequence, I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So just to be clear, when you said that on 22nd of May the Muslims were finally ready for the war and carried out an attack on the Serbs, that attack you're talking about is the killing of Drazenko Mihajlovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Your Honours want to take the break at the normal time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I was about to ask you how much longer you need just for planning purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Probably just 5 to 10 minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we will take a break after the conclusion of this witness's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic, if we can go to 65 ter 24614. I'd like to look at this document. Sorry, it will be coming up on the screen. This is an official note of an interview you had with the Rogatica police in 2004, and it records what you told the police on that occasion, and it talks about how you -- it says you were actually removed from your position as party president in March of 1992. And then, this is the third paragraph in the middle, it says: "After a certain period of time, he joined a JNA unit, the commander of which was Major Radomir Furtula. Veselinovic played the role of a rear soldier. He stayed with this unit until around September 1992, when the Executive Committee president appointed him head of the income administration on which position he remained until the end of 1993 ..." And the next paragraph at the bottom of the English it says: "Due to the fact that he was removed from the party president's office and because of his service in the military, he is not aware of the events surrounding the creation of the Crisis Staff or its later actions, and neither is he aware of its influence on the course of the military and police actions during 1992." The next paragraph says: "As far as the collection centres are concerned, considering that he was not present in the town in the period between March and September, he is aware of the existence of a collection centre at the secondary school but does not know any details about its creation or command structure." And then concludes by saying that: "He does not have any knowledge about the disappearance of 13 children from the municipality ..." Now, as you can see, this note says you served in Major Furtula's JNA unit from sometime around March 1992 until September 1992. We know that's not true. You testified today that you were in that unit for about a month, during April and May 1992. It states that after you served in this unit in September of 1992, you were appointed head of the income administration. That's also not true. You actually provided a copy of the decision appointing you director of revenue administration on the 30th of June, 1992. That's MFI D2961, referenced at paragraph 15 of your statement. And at paragraph 15 you also state that you were appointed to head of commission to accommodate refugees on the 30th of May, which is corroborated by another document you provided, D2960. And it also states that due to your service in the military, you were not aware of events surrounding the creation of the Crisis Staff or its later actions. That's also not true considering your evidence today, which provided details about the creation of the Crisis Staff, its functions, and your membership in it. And the note states that you were not present in the town between March and September 1992. Once again that is not true. You testified that you first entered the town five or six days after its liberation, which you stated was sometime in July, and that was at page 46 of today's transcript. And you actually videotaped that event are and we saw some footage of that. So, Mr. Veselinovic, in essence, you did not tell the truth to the Rogatica police when they interviewed you in 2004; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the policemen wrote in this official note. I told them the truth too. I could not have been in the JNA until September, because they had gone to Sarajevo. I stayed and left that unit before they left for Sarajevo. I don't know why they put September here. That's not what I told them. I told you after talking to prominent Serbs, long-time business leaders, inviting them to join the Crisis Staff, I left all the activities to Tomo Batinic and Mile Ujic, and I reported to a unit. While I was in the unit, the Municipal Board was appointed, the mandates were verified, the list of the members of the Crisis Staff was published. They informed me that I was a member and invited me to return. That's what I've said already. What they wrote here about the month of September, it must be their mistake, or maybe a typo. That's not what I stated to them. All these documents that I confirmed today are then refuted by this. All the -- all the decisions that I've shown you would be false. All the activities that I engaged in would all be denied by this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Veselinovic, it's not just a typo about your dates in the unit. It also states that you were not present in the town between March and September, and for that reason you don't know anything about the collection centres. It states that due to your service in the military, you have no information about the creation of the Crisis Staff or its later actions. So do you have any explanation for how the Rogatica police got this report of your interview with them so wrong in so many ways?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: They interviewed me, but this person wrote this subjectively. You know what perception can be. I was not in town. They believed that the Crisis Staff was outside of town, and it was, near the periphery. I had no need to go into the city. I did not know what the army was doing. I did not know what was going on in -- on military front lines. That's what they meant what they wrote that I did not --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This -- the interpretation of this answer is a disaster. Nothing is what the witness said. He talked about perception. He said not that he believed that it was outside of town, that -- he said he knows. He said that's what they meant when they said he did not go into town. This cannot be followed so bad -- so bad is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic, you accept that you were interviewed by the Rogatica police on the 16 of June, 2004, as this document states?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this document, and I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6129, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency, certainly. For instance, this document, I usually take it up from the last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long do you think it would last?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Five minutes probably, not more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then shall we conclude this witness's evidence and take a break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Veselinovic, while we're still on this document, did they let you read this document? Did you verify it with your signature?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember, but the talk was informal. We were sitting and talking. I presented them with certain facts. And later, after I left, they made this official note and signed it. How they perceived all the things I was saying, how completely askew it is, you can see for what is written. Before or after this conversation with them, I never got this paper to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under whose command were the Serbs who received weapons from the JNA, under the command of the Crisis Staff, the Territorial Defence, or a third party?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: All those who received weapons were under JNA command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I have to call up a document briefly. On page 66, it was put that Serbs attacked Rogatica on the 22nd of May or around that date. Who was attacking and who was defending themselves on that Sunday, 22nd May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the precise date when it happened, but if that is believed to be the date of the fighting in town when three Serb soldiers were killed, it was a total chaos after the killing of Drazenko Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who was the attacker? Who was attacking Rogatica? Who took over Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Rogatica was taken over by the Muslims. They were in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 65 ter 6968, dated 23rd June -- no. Can we see the one from the 29th first, 7088.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at this regular operative report dated 25th of June. In paragraph 5 it says up there who is where, and in paragraph 5 it says they carried out offensive actions against our positions in that area. Did the Serb army go into Rogatica before this definitive liberation?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: They couldn't. We couldn't walk around Rogatica saying, Now we won't shoot, now we will shoot. Quite simply, no Serb could go into Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And does this report correspond with what you know about the attacks and their deployment in Dub, Karacici, Golubovici and so on?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have no reason to doubt the report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2965, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Throughout the whole period, Dr. Veselinovic, until you liberated Rogatica, who carried out attacks?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: The attacks were carried out by Muslims from Rogatica. Since we were on the periphery, their objective -- and they strived to expand the territory and join up with the area of Gorazde with some villages of there that we were cutting off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 65 ter 6968 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is from the 23rd of June, and what it says here is that this is a regular operations report. The enemy continues being most active in the town on the Sjemec-Visegrad road, and it's firing at our positions. And in the sector of Gornja Aleska [phoen], the enemy attacked our forces which were securing the work being done on the power transmission line. Do you remember that, that they knocked down the power transmission line?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I don't know the particulars, but I know that specific in Rogatica they torched the transformer station. There was no electricity for a long time, and you could see their machine-gun nests on those photographs, and also you could see when they fired at houses, when they -- the ammunition fell short of their targets. And you also saw some other details, but I don't know about any particulars regarding activities out of town. I know only what I heard while I was working at Sladara during my activities in the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2966, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one more question, Dr. Veselinovic. Let's clarify this confusion about when the Serbs had which kind of weapons. After the JNA withdrew, did the Army of Republika Srpska have more weapons than the Serbs had before the JNA withdrew?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we have to know that the TO unit formed by Rajko Kusic was very quickly placed under the JNA by activities the Crisis Staff, and it became part of the Yugoslav People's Army. And as such, it was in a situation that it had more weaponry and it had a greater amount of weaponry at its disposal, as a unit, part of the force under the command of the General Staff headed by General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to read to you what Mr. Ujic said on page 33466. I'm going to read it in English so it could be translated better. Reply, line 21: [In English] "Please, I can't laconically say 'yes,' but just in a few words. I co-ordinated the artillery, as you know, so that the targets could be engaged from which we received fire. Only they were neutralised. That's the extent of my participation." [Interpretation] Do you have any knowledge or do you know if anyone shelled for the purpose of getting rid of the population, of driving the population out as it is suggested in this question?

utterances.speaker: SVETO VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, the horse has left the barn, but the witness in his cross-examination said he knew nothing about this attack, and it's completely improper for Dr. Karadzic to read somebody else's evidence to him and ask a question about it in that manner. There was no foundation for it. And just while I'm on my feet, Dr. Karadzic has now pointed to the precise passage that supported the question I put to the witness, which in my question I said that Mr. Ujic had given evidence that he co-ordinated this artillery attack, caused the population to flee, and resulted in the wounding of children. And at transcript page 33466 he -- at line 21 and 22, he said he co-ordinated the artillery --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it might have sounded that they -- that witness had agreed that shelling caused the fleeing of the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yeah, but in -- then at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on. I think it's enough.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Excellency. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Veselinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I just have to put this on the record. And then I asked Mr. Ujic: "And those children had been left behind the column of Muslims fleeing those villages; right?" And the answer was: "Yes, yes." I think the question was fair, and that's at line 16 of transcript page 33467.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's leave it there. Thank you, Ms. Gustafson, and thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Dr. Veselinovic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. And we'll rise all together. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.40.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was my pleasure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Deuric. Please make yourself comfortable. Before you start giving evidence, Mr. Deuric, I'd like to draw your attention to a particular Rule here at the International Tribunal. Do you hear me in the language you understand, Mr. Deuric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Under this Rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges, if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the power to compel you answer the question, but in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than for false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Deuric.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I just remind you to pause between question and answer, because we want to make sure that everything is correctly recorded in the transcript. If you follow the cursor on the monitor, when it stops after I put my question to you, then you can start your answer. Did you provide a statement to my team?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D7231 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, do you see the statement on the screen in front of you? Is that the statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read the statement, and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I read it and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the last page, please, so that the witness could identify the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature, Mr. Deuric?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And does the statement accurately reflect what you said? Did you hear me, Mr. Deuric? Is the statement correct? Is what is stated there a reflection of what you said?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today that the Defence team put to you when they took the statement, would your answers in essence be the same?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to tender this statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: There is none, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2967, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now going to read the summary of Mr. Deuric's statement in English. [In English] Momir Deuric was a security guard of the reception centre of Susica. He provided security for the depots at Susica which housed equipment for the Territorial Defence. At this time, the composition of the guards was mixed. However, Momir Deuric found that following his annual leave at the end of 1991, a Muslim colleague had been made chief of security despite being far less experienced than Momir Deuric. Up until the early 1990, Momir Deuric considers that there was no particular ethnic intolerance. However, at the beginning of the 1992, when the plan of the Muslims, Croats, and Slovenes to break up Yugoslavia came to light, the Serbs began to mistrust the Muslims. The Serbs were not in favour of this break-up, and when the national parties took charge, the situation started going downhill. Momir Deuric recalls that the Muslim SDA party in particular denigrated the other parties, and at their inaugural meetings there was an enormous outpouring of hatred towards the Serbs. Further, at the inaugural meeting of the SDS, the Muslims organised themselves and threw stones at vehicles and passers-by who were attending the meeting. Momir Deuric is aware that when the war in Croatia began, the Muslims supported the Croats and went to fight on their side. Clashes then between Serbs and Muslims became frequent. During 1991, the Serbs were mostly mobilised to the Territorial Defence units. However, the Muslims did not respond to this call-up. Through mobilisation, many Serbs obtained weapons, whereas the Muslims obtained them mainly via the SDA and bought them for money. In April 1992, Momir Deuric's two Muslim colleagues stopped attending work and therefore the Serbian guards had to organise themselves. At this time, there was already talk of fighting between Muslims and Serbs which caused great panic. People started leaving in droves. The majority of inhabitants had various kinds of weapons, and in the evenings shooting was often heard. He was aware that the Serb representatives in the municipal government in Vlasenica tried in various ways to avoid war with the Muslims. They proposed dividing the territory into two municipalities. The Muslims in authority accepted this decision. However, they immediately began leaving Vlasenica en masse. Momir Deuric recalls a complete mobilisation of the Serbs in Vlasenica was carried out on 21st of April, 1992. At this point, only one depot was full and therefore in May 1992, Serbs who had fled from -- fled other surrounding villages were accommodated in the empty depot which was then guarded by the police. Every day Serbs left this depot as accommodation was found for them in the city or elsewhere and soon the depot was empty. After the depot had been emptied, the army took control of it and started bringing Muslims to the depot from neighbouring towns. There were instances where Muslim families went to the depot to spend the night there until transport could be arranged as they did not feel safe in their own home. Momir Deuric was not aware of anyone being killed in the facility. He observed on several occasions that a foreign delegation arrived at the depot accompanied by the police. He later learned that these delegations were mainly from the International Red Cross. On 26th of September, 1992, Momir Deuric heard heavy gunfire early in the morning from the direction of Rogosija village and knew that the Muslims had attacked it. A call was made for people to go and assist in the village as many Serbs were wounded. He responded to this call and when he arrived, he saw that the village had been torched and many people were slaughtered, both soldiers and civilians. No Muslim fighters were found after this attack, as they had withdrawn immediately after committing this attack. Momir Deuric attended the funeral of those who had been killed in Rogosija and was not aware of any officials from Pale attending. A day or two after this funeral, the depot was closed as all the Muslims had been taken for an exchange. Momir Deuric did not hear from anyone that Radovan Karadzic gave any kind of orders to anyone in Vlasenica with regard to the treatment of Muslims. [Interpretation] This was the summary. I don't have questions for this witness at this point, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, as you have now noted, your evidence in this case has been admitted in its entirety in writing instead of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Deuric.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You told us in your statement that there was a complete mobilisation in Vlasenica on 21st of April, 1992. You were summoned to report to the premises of the Boksit company. Can you tell us who exactly did you go to report? Was it command of the Serb TO in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes. The TO command from Vlasenica. We received summons from the Secretariat for National Defence, and we reported to the Boksit building. And earlier it was agreed that Vlasenica be divided into two municipalities, Serbian one and a Muslim one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is in your statement. You don't have to repeat. It's okay. I'll just ask you specific questions.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And the TO assigned you to provide security to the TO facilities at Susica together with Slobodan Jovic and others, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You told us in paragraph 18 that after the army took control of Susica, they started bringing Muslims, but you didn't provide any date. This Chamber has heard evidence that the VRS established camp for prisoners at Susica on 31st May 1992. So this is the date when the army took over Susica, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: First of all, Serb families that had fled Gorazde, Olovo, and Kladanj came to the facility in Susica. They spent two or three nights there. The municipal authorities found --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is again in your statement. I'm just trying to find out the date. Is it 31st May 1992? If you remember. If you don't remember, it's okay. When the army took over Susica. We can move on. That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: First the police handled the security in Susica, and then I think in late May, it was the army that took over that job from the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is in P03240.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You told us, Mr. Deuric, that among the buildings at Susica, there was the old TO building that was used to store the TO equipment. There was the new TO building that you say was built in 1991 and there was the small guardhouse. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: These buildings were about 20 metres apart. They were surrounded by barbed wire fence and there were trenches around it. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was barbed wire, but it had been torn two or three years prior. It was very old wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at some photos of Susica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have in e-court 65 ter 24591.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, in this photo we see Susica camp from the air. The big frame on this photo is the building that you say was built in 1991. Next to it is the old TO building and opposite to these two is the small guardhouse. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is another view of Susica camp from the air. And here we can see other buildings and houses around Susica camp and there's the Vlasenica town in the background, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This shows the entrance to the Susica camp. To our right is the old TO building. Next to it is the new -- next to it is the new TO building, and the white guardhouse is the opposite side of the new building.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This photo was taken in 1996, whereas the previous photos, they were from 2002. This photo depicts the area behind the guardhouse; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is area in front of the new building, and here we can see an electric pole in the shape of the letter A. Can you confirm this pole was there in 1996 and before?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this again we see Susica camp from the air, and this pole is in the middle. That's correct, isn't it? Can you confirm that this is Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will tender these photos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6130, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You told us in your statement that you observed several times from your guardhouse that a foreign delegation visited Susica. When you say, Mr. Deuric, in your statement "guardhouse," you are referring to the guardhouse that we saw on the photos. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: No. From the warehouse where I worked there was materiel and equipment of the TO or of its Municipal Staff. I was there most of the time storing and sorting equipment which would be strewn about every time soldiers came by. On occasion, I could observe from the warehouse that a delegation has arrived. Later on, people told me they were from the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I was referring what you said in your statement. Now you were saying you were in this old TO building that we also saw on the photos. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Would the prisoners be present at Susica while these delegations were coming?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: How much -- how many of them would be there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: The captured people?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Well, it depended. There were more when buses arrived to take them to be exchanged. I know that a group went to Batkovic. I think there were two buses that went there. Later there were fewer. The International Red Cross mission visited prior to their being sent for an exchange and afterwards too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the report prepared by the CSC mission that visited Susica on 2nd September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have P03228.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Second paragraph of the report refers to two sheds, one of which was larger and was used to hold detainees. The second shed, they say, was smaller and was used to store boxes of small arms, old shoes, and other military equipment. Empty boxes were piled outside the small shed, they say. Paragraphs after refer to prisoners and general conditions at Susica. Do you remember this visit of 2nd September 1992, Mr. Deuric?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. I wasn't present at that time. As for the shack that was there, we only --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We can move on. According to this report, the delegation was able to see about 40 prisoners. At the end of the third paragraph, they say they were not confident that they saw all of the prisoners. Do you know, Mr. Deuric, where other prisoners were during this visit?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I know that sometimes in the morning, although not every day, people reported for work, people such as plumbers, electricians. Whenever something needed to be done. For the most part they went to work in the health clinic when things needed to be fixed such as plumbing, and that is why they may not have been present. They weren't there all day long at Susica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now I would like to show you a few photos that this delegation was able at to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 26 -- 24615. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is the entrance to the Susica camp. We see the gate, the old TO building that -- with boxes piled in front of it. And there is a new -- the new building. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This photo shows inside of the new TO building. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The person that looks towards camera was Hasan Paric [phoen], prisoner at Susica. Do you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This shows inside of the old TO building described in the report that you say you were guarding. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So you were guarding this without knowing what was happening outside. Is that your evidence, Mr. Deuric?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: This is not the old building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's what they say in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender these photos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6131, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, you say in paragraph 19 that you were not aware of anyone being killed at Susica. In fact, what was happening at Susica were murders, beatings, torture, and rapes. This is what was taking place, Mr. Deuric, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: I wasn't at Susica every day. I have children and a wife, and they were refugees in Serbia. When I was at Susica, no one was killed in my presence. I wasn't able to hear or see it. I heard from my comrades that two people died, Durmo Handzic and Zivzic [phoen]. I don't remember his first name. I do remember that doctors came and confirmed that they died of heart attack. That's what I know positively.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic pled guilty to crimes in Susica, and you -- you saw him torturing and nearly killing a prisoner in Susica, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We have a witness statement of a Muslim prisoner who was tortured by Nikolic. That person, a colleague of yours, with whom you had spent years before the war guarding this same location, stated that when you entered the new building while Dragan Nikolic was pushing gun to his throat, Nikolic stopped, and he thinks that his life was saved. Do you remember this, Mr. Deuric?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 24589, and not to be broadcast. You will see the first page of the statement and we need page 7. Can we have page 7? Second-last paragraph in English and sixth last in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You can read it for yourself, Mr. Deuric. The reality is, Mr. Deuric, you knew that Dragan Nikolic tortured prisoners, and that was committed by other guards as well, but you're simply not willing to tell that to this Court, isn't it? You see your name there. It's like sixth paragraph from the bottom. You read it? After the same page this witness refers to Veljko Basic and Slobodan Pajic, who, according to this witness, took a bus load of women and children out of Susica, and they were never returned. You told us about Veljko Basic in your statement. Slobodan Pajic was a VRS officer --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Slobodan Pajic was a VRS officer who was present at Susica, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Veljko Basic was the camp warden. Dragan Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Did you report to Slobodan Pajic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: -- was trying to be imposing. He had a finger in every pie. I was nobody. I couldn't report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Another witness, Mr. Deuric, saw you outside the new building among Dragan Nikolic, Radenko Kovacevic, Goran Viskovic and Predrag Bastah. You were making lists of new prisoners and those who were taken out for forced labour and exchange. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please establish first whether the witness actually managed to read the paragraph where his name can be found. I don't think we were able to indicate to him clearly where it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's fair enough. Mr. Robinson, did you have an observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, that was my exact point, that the witness never had the opportunity to comment on the question that was put to him about that individual whose name appears in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I thought it takes time for the witness to read and I wasn't sure whether he's reading. I moved on, but we can certainly do that. Can we go up the page. Perhaps down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So this is the big paragraph in this statement when this colleague of yours said that Nikolic was pushing gun to his throat and you entered the big, new building. Do you see that, Mr. Deuric?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him put his rifle into his mouth, but I met Jenki on his way out of the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So you were in the new building --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Perhaps he thought he saw me and then he went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is nothing of this is in your statement, Mr. Deuric. You're telling us that now.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: You want me to recall it after 20 years?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: As I mentioned to you, another witness saw you making list of prisoners at Susica. Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Who made the list? No. I never did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 24590.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it should not be broadcast, and we should establish whether the man -- the witness actually recognises who the person giving this statement is that he referred to as a friend.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There was an overlap and we did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before I clarify with the witness, what was the reason why we should not broadcast the previous document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Simply out of abundance of caution with Mr. -- Mr. President. Simply we don't have any information about this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, after Mr. Karadzic referred to "a friend," what did you say? We didn't hear that because it was not interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know which friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we blow up the bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Do you see now your name? It says Momir -- Deuric Momir, known as Momo, Kovacevic Radenko, Viskovic Goran, Predrag Bastah. And after that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid we need to show the witness the first statement first and then the second so that he would know who provided that statement. The witness didn't see who the person is that is being referred to as friend and now he doesn't seem to know who it is who actually entered.
